1.b4.name: Sokolsky Opening
1.b4.background: Named after the Soviet player Alexei Sokolsky (1908–1969), whose 1963 monograph defended it. Also called the Polish Opening, and the Orangutan after Tartakower, who claimed that an orangutan at the Bronx Zoo had advised the move before his game against Maróczy at New York 1924.

1.b4 e5.strategy: Takes a share of the centre at once and opens the diagonal of the f8-bishop toward the b4-pawn, so White has to decide how to treat its flank pawn. The most natural reply: Black stakes a claim in the middle while White has so far only gained queenside space.

1.b4 d5.name: Sokolsky Opening, with d5
1.b4 d5.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn that the bishop on b2 will not hit, and gives up the attack on b4 in exchange. Black gets a classical, comfortable set-up, and White has to show what the early b-pawn move was for.

1.b4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and watches e4 and d5 without committing a pawn, so Black can still choose between a solid centre and a fianchetto of its own. A flexible reply that leaves White's flank play without a clear target.

1.b4 c6.name: Sokolsky Opening: Outflank Variation
1.b4 c6.strategy: Prepares to attack the b4-pawn from the flank with the queen or the a-pawn, and keeps the centre pawns flexible. It is a slow, solid reply that asks White to say how the b-pawn is to be kept.

1.b4 e6.strategy: Prepares a solid centre and frees the f8-bishop toward b4 without putting a pawn in the way of the fianchettoed bishop. Taking the b-pawn once White's bishop is on b2 would be a trap for Black: the bishop takes g7 and wins the rook on h8.

1.b4 c5.name: Sokolsky Opening: Birmingham Gambit
1.b4 c5.strategy: A sharp pawn offer that challenges the b-pawn at once. If White takes, Black has given a pawn for pressure on the c5 square and for play against White's loosened queenside; the move pulls the game out of the usual paths at a real price.

1.b4 f5.name: Sokolsky Opening: Dutch Defence
1.b4 f5.strategy: Takes control of e4 with the f-pawn and aims for an aggressive set-up on the kingside. The cost is a looser king position, and the bishop on b2 will look down the long diagonal toward g7.

1.b4 Nc6.name: Sokolsky Opening: Grigorian Variation
1.b4 Nc6.strategy: Develops and attacks the b4-pawn, but the knight stands where a pawn advance with b5 drives it away with a gain of time. Black fights for the centre with pieces, at the cost of spending tempi on this one.

1.b4 Nh6.name: Sokolsky Opening: Karniewski Variation
1.b4 Nh6.strategy: A knight on the rim, aimed at f5 and g4, which keeps the e- and f-pawns free. It does nothing for the centre and the knight is awkwardly placed, so White can build up at leisure.

1.b4 b5.name: Sokolsky Opening: Symmetrical Variation
1.b4 b5.strategy: Mirrors White's move and claims queenside space, but spends a move on a flank pawn while White still has the first word in the centre. The two b-pawns face each other and the game becomes a manoeuvring one in which White keeps the small edge of the first move.

1.b4 c6 2.Bb2.strategy: Completes the idea of the opening: the bishop takes the long diagonal toward Black's kingside. The b4-pawn has no pawn protection, so White must be ready to advance or support it when Black attacks it from the flank.

1.b4 c6 2.a3.strategy: Supports the b-pawn with the rook-pawn, so Black's flank attack on it finds nothing to take. The price is a tempo spent on a pawn move while Black builds the centre, and the bishop has still to find its diagonal.

1.b4 c6 2.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop and leaves the fianchetto for later, but leaves the b4-pawn without support: a queen or rook-pawn attack on it gains Black time, since White must defend or advance the pawn. Sound but slow, and Black gets the larger share of the centre.

1.b4 c6 2.Bb2 a5.strategy: Attacks the b4-pawn with the a-pawn and forces White to decide at once whether to advance it, support it or give it up. Black contests White's space on the flank instead of the centre, at the cost of loosening its own queenside.

1.b4 c6 2.Bb2 Qb6.strategy: Attacks the b4-pawn, which the bishop on b2 does not protect, and makes White deal with it before developing further. Black sets the pace on the queenside; the cost is an early queen move that gains little if White simply defends the pawn.

1.b4 c6 2.Bb2 d5.strategy: Takes the centre and ignores the flank: with c6 and d5 Black builds a solid pawn pair and can develop freely behind it. The b4-pawn stays a target for later, but Black is not forced to attack it now.

1.b4 c6 2.Bb2 a5 3.b5.name: Sokolsky Opening: Outflank Variation, Schuehler Gambit
1.b4 c6 2.Bb2 a5 3.b5.strategy: Pushes the attacked pawn forward and offers it as a gambit: if Black takes, White gets open lines and a lead in development for the pawn. If Black declines, White keeps the space on the queenside, but the pawn on b5 is then hard to hold.

1.b4 c6 2.Bb2 a5 3.a3.strategy: Meets the attack by offering a trade: if Black takes, the a-file opens, the rooks can come off and White has the pawn back on b4 with a solid queenside. Safe and flexible, but it gives up the space the b-pawn could have claimed.

1.b4 c6 2.Bb2 a5 3.bxa5.strategy: Takes the attacking pawn: after ...Rxa5 the pawns are level and Black's rook uses the half-open a-file, while White has given up its space gain. Safe but passive, since the queenside advance has achieved nothing.

1.b4 c6 2.Bb2 a5 3.b5 cxb5.strategy: Accepts the gambit: Black wins a pawn and removes White's queenside space. In return White gets open lines and a lead in development, so Black's task is to complete its own development safely before the extra pawn can be used.

1.b4 c6 2.Bb2 a5 3.b5 c5.strategy: Declines the pawn and fixes the queenside: the pawn on b5 keeps White's space, but it stays loose and needs support, and Black avoids opening lines against its undeveloped pieces. Sound, if less ambitious than taking the pawn.

1.b4 c6 2.Bb2 a5 3.b5 d5.strategy: Ignores the offered pawn and takes the centre. If White takes on c6, Black recaptures with a developing move and the material stays level, but White gets an half-open b-file and Black has let the free pawn go.

1.b4 c6 2.Bb2 a5 3.b5 cxb5 4.e4.name: Sokolsky Opening: Schuehler Gambit
1.b4 c6 2.Bb2 a5 3.b5 cxb5 4.e4.strategy: Takes the centre and opens the f1-bishop at once: the loose pawn on b5 is attacked, and Bxb5 would pin the d7-pawn against the king. White pays a pawn for the initiative, and open lines and a lead in development are the best compensation the position offers.

1.b4 c6 2.Bb2 a5 3.b5 cxb5 4.a4.strategy: Attacks the b5-pawn with the rook-pawn to win back the sacrificed pawn. Black can answer by pushing it on, or by taking and giving it back; either way White spends a tempo on the flank with its pieces undeveloped and is still a pawn down.

1.b4 c6 2.Bb2 a5 3.b5 cxb5 4.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop to win the b5-pawn back and keeps the pawn structure compact. It does not fight for the centre, so Black has time to support or advance the extra pawn, and White is left a pawn down with only a modest lead in development.

1.b4 d5 2.Bb2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop takes the long diagonal toward g7 and the kingside. The main line, in which White accepts that Black holds more of the centre and plays against it from the wings.

1.b4 d5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight to guard e5 and d4 before the bishop is committed, a patient move order that leaves White's choices open. The b4-pawn has no defender yet, but nothing attacks it either.

1.b4 d5 2.e3.strategy: A quiet developing move that opens the f1-bishop and leaves the fianchetto for later. It stakes no claim in the centre, so Black's d-pawn holds the middle unchallenged and White's plan stays slow.

1.b4 d5 2.Bb2 Nf6.strategy: Develops and adds a second guard to the centre, the standard reply: Black asks White to commit while its own set-up stays flexible. Black owns more of the centre, and White bets on the long diagonal and on pressure against it.

1.b4 d5 2.Bb2 Bf5.name: Sokolsky Opening: Baltic Defence
1.b4 d5 2.Bb2 Bf5.strategy: Gets the light-squared bishop out before a pawn on e6 can close it in, and its diagonal points at the c2 square in White's camp. A sound, active way to develop that does not weaken the pawn centre.

1.b4 d5 2.Bb2 c6.strategy: Backs the d5-pawn with another pawn and builds a compact centre with no target for the bishop on b2. Slow but solid, and the c8-bishop stays free to develop outside the chain.

1.b4 d5 2.Bb2 Qd6.name: Sokolsky Opening: German Defence
1.b4 d5 2.Bb2 Qd6.strategy: Attacks the undefended b4-pawn and prepares to support a pawn on e5 in one move, but puts the queen out early where it can become a target. White can defend calmly and carry on developing, so Black has made a point without a lasting gain.

1.b4 d5 2.Bb2 c6 3.a4.name: Sokolsky Opening: Myers Variation
1.b4 d5 2.Bb2 c6 3.a4.strategy: Gains queenside space with the rook-pawn ready to support a push of the b-pawn. It spends a move on the flank while Black has already built its centre, and the b4-pawn still has no pawn protection.

1.b4 d5 2.Bb2 c6 3.e3.strategy: Builds a compact, flexible centre: the pawn supports d4 and frees the f1-bishop, so White develops without weakening anything. White accepts that Black holds the larger share of the centre and plays a slow game, with the long-diagonal bishop as its main asset.

1.b4 d5 2.Bb2 c6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight to guard e5 and d4, so Black's central pawns cannot advance easily, and leaves the pawn structure open. A patient move that keeps all options, though Black's queen can already take aim at the b4-pawn.

1.b4 d5 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.Nf3.name: Sokolsky Opening, with d5
1.b4 d5 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.Nf3.strategy: Brings the knight to where it guards e5 and d4. White has a flexible, patient game: space on the queenside, a bishop on the long diagonal and no commitment in the centre.

1.b4 d5 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.e3.strategy: Builds a solid, flexible centre: the pawn supports d4 and frees the f1-bishop, so White develops without weakening anything. White gives Black the larger share of the centre and plays for a slow, manoeuvring game around the long-diagonal bishop.

1.b4 d5 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.a3.strategy: Guards the b4-pawn with the rook-pawn so that it cannot be attacked for free, at the price of a tempo on a move that does not develop a piece. Sound but passive: Black develops freely and keeps the centre.

1.b4 e5 2.Bb2.strategy: The main line: the bishop takes the long diagonal and attacks the pawn on e5, accepting that the b4-pawn is exposed. White reckons that a central pawn is worth more than a flank pawn, so it gladly trades one for the other.

1.b4 e5 2.a3.name: Sokolsky Opening: Bugayev Attack
1.b4 e5 2.a3.strategy: Protects the b4-pawn directly, so the f8-bishop cannot win it, and puts off the decision on the bishop. White keeps a solid queenside chain at the price of a tempo, while Black gets the centre and an easy start.

1.b4 e5 2.b5.strategy: Moves the pawn out of the f8-bishop's reach and gains space, but it is the second move with the same pawn and Black takes the centre at once. The advanced pawn is difficult to defend, and the position is level at best for White.

1.b4 e5 2.Bb2 f6.strategy: Defends the e5 pawn with the f-pawn, which blocks the long diagonal, and keeps the bishop's option of taking on b4. The price is a weaker king: the f6 square is taken from the knight and the diagonal toward the king is open.

1.b4 e5 2.Bb2 d6.name: Sokolsky Opening: Czech Defence
1.b4 e5 2.Bb2 d6.strategy: Defends the e5 pawn with a pawn and closes the f8-bishop's diagonal toward b4, so the pawn is no longer attacked. A solid choice that builds a firm centre and takes the sting from the bishop on b2.

1.b4 e5 2.Bb2 c5.name: Sokolsky Opening: Wolferts Gambit
1.b4 e5 2.Bb2 c5.strategy: Attacks the b4-pawn but leaves the e5-pawn hanging to the bishop on b2. White can take on c5 first and then on e5 and be a pawn up; even if the b-pawn falls instead, Black has traded its central pawn for a flank pawn, which favours White.

1.b4 e5 2.Bb2 Bxb4.strategy: Takes the flank pawn, and White takes the e5 pawn in return. White then has the central pawn and Black the faster development; the position is roughly level, perhaps a shade better for White, and the fight is between the extra centre and Black's activity.

1.b4 e5 2.Bb2 f6 3.b5.name: Sokolsky Opening: Bugayev Advance Variation
1.b4 e5 2.Bb2 f6 3.b5.strategy: Moves the pawn out of reach of the f8-bishop and claims queenside space. The pawn is now far advanced and hard to protect, so White accepts a long-term target in return for the space and a safe bishop.

1.b4 e5 2.Bb2 f6 3.e4.name: Sokolsky Opening: Tartakower Gambit
1.b4 e5 2.Bb2 f6 3.e4.strategy: Leaves the b4-pawn to the f8-bishop and takes the centre instead: White plays for development and open lines against the king that ...f6 has weakened. It costs a real pawn, so the gambit works only if the attack comes quickly.

1.b4 e5 2.Bb2 f6 3.a3.strategy: Guards the b4-pawn with the rook-pawn, so the f8-bishop has nothing to take, and keeps the bishop's diagonal and the pawn chain intact. A solid reply that costs a tempo and leaves White to exploit the weakened kingside by normal development.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto and, with the bishop on the long diagonal, makes taking on b4 a mistake: the bishop takes g7 and wins the rook on h8. White's flank pawn is safe for now and the bishop watches the whole diagonal.

1.b4 e6 2.a3.strategy: Protects the b4-pawn with the rook-pawn before the f8-bishop can take it, and keeps the choice of fianchetto for later. Solid and flexible; the price is a tempo, and Black may take the centre.

1.b4 e6 2.b5.strategy: Moves the pawn out of reach of the f8-bishop and claims queenside space at once. But the pawn is far from home and without support, an easy target for ...a6 or ...c6, and Black gets time to build the centre.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6.strategy: Develops and controls the e4 and d5 squares without committing a pawn. Black can still choose between a solid pawn centre and a fianchetto of its own, and White's fianchetto has no direct target.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 d5.strategy: Takes the centre with a second pawn and fixes a solid structure. The c8-bishop stays shut in behind e6 for now and the b4-pawn is left for later, but the game is calm and Black plays against White's slow queenside advance.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 b6.strategy: Answers the fianchetto with one of its own, so the c8-bishop gets its own long diagonal. Flexible and solid, but it claims no part of the centre and lets White choose the pawn structure.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5.strategy: Answers the one concrete problem of the position: the b4-pawn is attacked by Black's bishop and nothing defends it. Stepping forward takes it out of reach and gains space, and commits White to a cramping pawn on b5 that must now be kept safe.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.a3.strategy: Defends the b4-pawn with the rook's pawn, so taking it with the bishop would only lose the bishop for a pawn. White keeps the pawn on b4 instead of pushing it, but spends a tempo on defence and leaves the pawn open to being challenged by ...a5.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.c3.strategy: Defends the b4-pawn with the c-pawn, but the pawn lands on the bishop's own diagonal and shuts out the very piece that was developed to b2. White holds the pawn at the price of its most active piece.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 d5.strategy: Takes the full centre with pawns on d5 and e6 and ignores the pawn on b5. Black builds a solid, classical structure and keeps the king's bishop free, so White's space gain on the wing has to be justified by pressure on the centre.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 a6.name: Sokolsky Opening: Queenside Defence
1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 a6.strategy: Challenges the advanced pawn at once: White must support it or let it be traded off. If the pawns come off, Black opens the a-file, at the price of committing the a-pawn to the fight.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 b6.name: Sokolsky Opening: Queen's Indian Variation
1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 b6.strategy: Puts the pawn directly in front of White's and prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop. Sound, but passive: White's advanced pawn keeps its grip on the queenside and Black has given it nothing to attack.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 a6 4.a4.strategy: Defends the pawn with the rook's pawn and keeps the space it has gained. White accepts that Black can trade on b5, which opens the a-file, rather than give the advanced pawn up or retreat it.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 a6 4.e3.strategy: Opens the diagonal for the king's bishop, which now guards b5 and recaptures there if Black trades. White gives up the idea of holding the advanced pawn with a pawn and settles for a sound, quiet development, while the a2-pawn keeps the a-file closed for Black's rook.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 a6 4.bxa6.strategy: Takes the pawn that challenges b5, so the space won by 3.b5 is traded away for Black's rook pawn at once. The b-file is half open for White, but Black recaptures with the b-pawn, the knight or the rook and has a comfortable game with no queenside cramp to fear.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 a6 4.a4 axb5.strategy: Trades pawns by taking on b5. After White recaptures, the a-file is open and the rooks face each other, so the game turns on who controls the file.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 a6 4.a4 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once, with the pawn controlling c4 and e4, and leaves the queenside tension in place for later. A solid answer that meets White's flank play with central control.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 a6 4.a4 c5.strategy: Challenges the centre and puts the question to the b5-pawn at once: White can take on a6, or en passant on c6, and either way the pawn that cramped Black is traded off. Black develops freely, but White decides how the queenside opens.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 a6 4.a4 axb5 5.ax.strategy: Recaptures so that the pawn stays on b5, still cramping Black's queenside, and leaves the rooks staring at each other down the open file. White keeps the space, but the pawn on b5 now has no pawn to support it.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 a6 4.a4 axb5 5.Nc.strategy: Develops instead of recapturing, and White is a pawn down for it: Black takes on a4 or pushes the pawn forward with a gain of time against the knight, and keeps the extra pawn. The knight also stands on the bishop's diagonal and blocks it.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 a6 4.a4 axb5 5.Bx.strategy: Trades the bishop for the knight while still a pawn down, and the queen's recapture on f6 attacks the rook on a1 along the long diagonal, where nothing defends it. White has to give up more material or a tempo to save the rook.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 a6 4.a4 axb5 5.ax.strategy: Trades off the rooks on the open file before White can use it; the bishop recaptures, so the trade is even and the file is left empty.
Tries to block the file with the knight, but the rook takes it: after Rxa6 Rxa6 bxa6 bxa6 Black has lost a knight for a pawn.
Ignores the attack on the rook on a8, which nothing defends: White takes it with Rxa8 and Black has no recapture, since the bishop and knight block the queen's path.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 a6 4.a4 axb5 5.ax.name: Sokolsky Opening: Rooks Swap Line
1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 a6 4.a4 axb5 5.ax.strategy: The natural recapture: the bishop is the only piece that can take, and it stays on the long diagonal where it keeps pressure on the knight on f6. White enters a quiet middlegame with the advanced pawn on b5 as its space asset.
Takes the knight instead of the rook, and Black simply retakes with the queen: White has lost a rook for nothing, and the rook on a1 still attacks the knight on b1.
Moves the knight away without recapturing, and the rook on a1 takes the queen with check: Rxd1+. White can only take the rook back, so it is a whole queen down.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 d5 4.e3.name: Sokolsky Opening: Schiffler-Sokolsky Variation
1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 d5 4.e3.strategy: A solid reply that opens the king's bishop, which now defends the pawn on b5, and prepares to castle. White accepts a quiet game: the bishop on b2 eyes the knight on f6 but wins nothing there, so the pawn on b5 must prove its worth with slow pressure.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 d5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight toward the centre and does not hurry to support b5: no Black piece attacks it yet, so White can finish development first. A flexible, sound set-up that keeps the king's bishop free to choose its square.

1.b4 e6 2.Bb2 Nf6 3.b5 d5 4.a4.strategy: Supports the b5-pawn with the rook's pawn before Black can attack it, building a firm queenside chain. It costs a tempo on the flank while Black develops in the centre, so White gains space but gives Black time.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2.strategy: Develops the bishop to the long diagonal, which the b-pawn's advance was meant to open, and aims it at the heart of Black's position. It commits White to a flank opening that fights for the centre from a distance.

1.b4 Nf6 2.c4.strategy: Adds a central pawn on the other wing, fighting for d5 and building a broad queenside pawn front with the b-pawn already advanced. The pawn on b4 has no defender yet, so White must watch for Black's attack on it by ...e6.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight first and keeps the choice of set-up open: the bishop can still go to b2, or the king's bishop can be fianchettoed. It is safe, but it gives Black time to prepare an attack on the b4-pawn.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6.name: Sokolsky Opening: King's Indian Variation
1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6.strategy: Black prepares a kingside fianchetto, so that the king's bishop can contest the long diagonal against White's bishop. Once it stands on g7, the knight on f6 is the only piece between the two bishops, and Black builds a compact, flexible position rather than fighting for the centre at once.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 e6.strategy: Opens the diagonal for the king's bishop, which now attacks the b4-pawn, so White must advance or defend it at once. Black builds a flexible, solid centre and develops with tempo, the usual way to meet White's flank opening.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 d5.strategy: Takes space in the centre at once and leaves the e-pawn's decision for later. The king's bishop stays shut in for now, so the b4-pawn is not yet attacked: a classical, solid set-up that answers flank play with central control.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.c4.strategy: Builds a wide queenside pawn front with the b- and c-pawns and controls d5, which discourages Black from striking in the centre. White commits to a space-grabbing plan, with the bishop on b2 as the long-range support.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.e4.name: Sokolsky Opening: King's Indian Variation, Schiffler Attack
1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.e4.strategy: Claims the centre at once and sets a trap: if Black takes with 3...Nxe4, then 4.Bxh8 wins the rook, since the knight has left f6 and the g-pawn has left g7. If Black simply declines, White has space but no more than that, and the e-pawn is left to be defended.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight to cover d4 and e5 and prepares to castle, while leaving the choice of pawn set-up for later. White keeps the long diagonal open for the b2-bishop and lets Black declare its plan: a flexible, safe move that stakes less space than the c-pawn.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.e3.strategy: Opens the king's bishop and supports a later central advance. It is solid but slow: it claims no space in the centre, and the b4-pawn still has no pawn protection, so White has to keep an eye on it while Black completes the fianchetto.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.c4 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto and faces White's bishop along the long diagonal, with only the knight between them. Black stays compact and delays the central fight, keeping the choice of how to challenge White's space for later.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.c4 d6.strategy: Controls e5 and frees the c8-bishop, building the compact pawn structure that goes with a fianchettoed bishop. If White trades the b2-bishop for the knight, Black recaptures with the e-pawn and accepts doubled f-pawns for a half-open e-file.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.c4 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop with an attack on the b4-pawn, which no pawn protects, so White must spend a move on it. It belongs to a different plan than the fianchetto: Black prepares a central pawn advance on d5, so the fianchetto stays unfinished for now.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.c4 Bg7 4.e3.strategy: Opens the king's bishop and supports a later central advance, which is the point of the setup. It is solid rather than ambitious: White prepares to develop the kingside and castle before committing the centre pawns.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.c4 Bg7 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight to cover d4 and e5 and prepares castling. It keeps the choice of central pawn structure open and lets Black show its plan first, a safe move that reaches the same set-ups as the quiet pawn move.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.c4 Bg7 4.g3.strategy: Fianchettoes the second bishop, so both of White's bishops press along the long diagonals. A sound, restrained set-up, but it leaves the centre unclaimed and keeps the knight and the d-pawn undeveloped for now.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.c4 Bg7 4.e3 d6.strategy: Gives the centre a solid base, controls e5 and frees the c8-bishop. Black builds the compact pawn structure this fianchetto wants, content to wait until White has shown where the space will be used.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.c4 Bg7 4.e3 O-O.strategy: Brings the king to safety and guards the g7-bishop, which frees the f6-knight to move: without castling, the knight cannot leave, because the white bishop would take on g7 and attack the rook. Black keeps the centre flexible and waits to see where White uses the space.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.c4 Bg7 4.e3 b6.strategy: Prepares a second fianchetto, so both black bishops will watch the long diagonal against White's queenside and the b2-bishop. A sound but slow plan: Black delays castling while the g7-bishop stays shut behind the knight.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.c4 Bg7 4.e3 d6 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight to a square from which it watches both d4 and e5, and prepares kingside castling. White now has the pieces in place to occupy the centre with a pawn.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.c4 Bg7 4.e3 d6 5.d4.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn at once, backed by the e-pawn, and gets a firm grip on e5 and c5. The cost is that the pawn blocks the b2-bishop on its long diagonal, the piece this opening is built around.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.c4 Bg7 4.e3 d6 5.Be2.strategy: A quiet developing move that prepares castling without deciding the pawn structure. It is a little passive: White waits to see where Black strikes, and the b4-pawn still has no pawn support.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.c4 Bg7 4.e3 d6 5.Nf3.strategy: Brings the king to safety and the rook to the f-file. Black's position is solid and ready for a pawn lever against the white centre.

Strikes at the b4-pawn, which no pawn protects, to open lines on the queenside. If White takes, the d-pawn recaptures and Black gets an open d-file and a queenside pawn for the b-pawn; if White pushes on with b5, the queenside closes and White has gained space.

Develops the knight and gives a second defender to e5, so Black can later break in the centre with the e-pawn. It is sound, but the knight blocks the c8-bishop, and the g7-bishop stays shut behind the f6-knight for the moment.

1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.c4 Bg7 4.e3 d6 5.Nf3.name: Sokolsky Opening: King's Indian Variation, Sokolsky Attack
1.b4 Nf6 2.Bb2 g6 3.c4 Bg7 4.e3 d6 5.Nf3.strategy: Completes a broad pawn front on b4, c4 and d4 and claims a large share of the space. It commits White to holding that centre, while Black will aim to undermine it with a pawn lever; the b4-pawn has no pawn support of its own.

Develops the bishop and clears the way to castle, leaving the d-pawn flexible: White can still choose between a broad centre and a lighter set-up. A restrained, solid move that keeps the pieces behind the pawns and claims less space than the pawn advance.

Adds a developing piece to the centre, eyeing d5 and e4, but the knight blocks the b2-bishop's diagonal and stands where the g7-bishop aims once the f6-knight moves, so Black can challenge it at once with ...Ne4.
